model.name: Identifier Scheme
model.purpose: Describe identifier schemes and namespaces as first-class governed objects: who establishes a scheme, what syntax and integrity rules constrain identifiers, how names are assigned to referents, how they are resolved or deactivated, and how they are crosswalked between schemes so that identifier drift, collision and reuse can be handled once at scheme level rather than inside every consuming model.
model.scope_statement: This mixin covers the scheme itself, its registration authority and delegated namespaces, lexical and checksum constraints, assignment and uniqueness policy, identifier lifecycle including rare reuse, retirement, split, merge and deactivation cases, resolution and dereference services, and declared mappings or embeddings between schemes. It does not model the identified referent, the organisation that happens to be a registrar, the network endpoint as a generic service, or storage and interface projections.
in_scope: Named identifier schemes, URI schemes, URN namespaces, DID methods and other managed identifier systems with a common definition and assignment process.
Registration authorities, change controllers, designated experts, International Code Designators and delegated sub-namespaces such as DOI prefixes, Handle prefixes, ARK NAANs and OID arcs.
Lexical syntax, ABNF or equivalent rules, check digits, canonicalisation, percent-encoding, case folding and scheme-specific equivalence.
Assignment of identifiers to referents, uniqueness and persistence policy, granularity, qualifiers, parts and variants.
Identifier status and events including reservation, issuance, temporary use, retirement, reassignment where permitted, deactivation, versioning and historical resolution.
Resolution and dereference services, multi-target resolution, metadata-only resolution, access-controlled resolution and resolver coverage.
Cross-scheme mapping, embedding of one scheme inside another, compact and fully qualified forms, and notation codes used as identifiers within a scheme.
out_of_scope: The identified referent itself (person, organisation, document, dataset, product, concept or location); those belong in sibling entity models that MIX-IN this scheme.
Generic organisation, party, contract, service-endpoint, access-control and records-retention models except as references from registrar, assigner, resolver operator and registration contract.
Formal ontology or metamodel registration of a scheme grammar as a conceptual model; that belongs in a model or ontology sibling.
Storage formats and access interfaces such as JSON, YAML, Markdown, HTML, Git, MCP and MongoDB, which are projections of this model, not semantics.
National civil-status identifiers, biometric templates and classified intelligence identifiers as domain content; only the scheme rules that would govern such systems if registered.
Protocol operations that merely use an identifier as a locator, except where the scheme definition itself specifies those operations.

boundary_notes.distinction: A registration authority, assigner or resolver operator is an organisation or party. This model records only the mandate, ICD, change-controller role and delegation chain relative to a scheme, and references the party record for legal identity.

A resolver is a service with endpoints, protocols and service levels. This model records scheme-specific resolution behaviour, coverage and PID-framework requirements, and references the service record for generic hosting.

A scheme ABNF, naming convention or concept scheme may itself be registered as a model. This mixin treats that artefact as a syntax or mapping constraint of the identifier scheme, not as ontology stewardship.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Access, ownership and audit service layers
boundary_notes.distinction: Who may read assignment records, bulk crosswalks or resolution logs is governed by catalogue ownership and access models. This mixin states identifier-specific privacy, security and audit requirements but does not redefine access control.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Document, dataset, product, person and location entity models
boundary_notes.distinction: Those models carry identifier values plus a scheme reference. This mixin is the scheme register that makes drift, collision, checksum and resolution behaviour detectable across the catalogue.

sources.title: RFC 8141: Uniform Resource Names (URNs)
sources.relevance: Normative URN syntax, NID and NSS, formal versus informal namespaces, uniqueness and non-reassignment, assignment process, equivalence ignoring r/q/f-components, resolution semantics and IANA NID registration template.

sources.title: RFC 3986: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax
sources.relevance: Generic URI syntax, scheme federation, percent-encoding, reserved characters, resolution versus dereference, relative references, normalisation ladder and security considerations for identifiers.

sources.title: RFC 7595: Guidelines and Registration Procedures for URI Schemes
sources.relevance: Permanent, provisional and historical URI scheme status, registration template, change controller, private reverse-domain schemes, operations definition, IRI sharing of the URI scheme registry, and security and privacy analysis requirements.

sources.title: Uniform Resource Names (URN) Namespaces
sources.relevance: Authoritative live register of formal and informal URN NIDs, expert-review procedure under RFC 8141, and pointers to namespace templates for isbn, doi, uuid, gs1, lei, oid and others.

sources.title: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes
sources.relevance: Authoritative live register of permanent, provisional and historical URI schemes with status, references, well-known URI support and designated experts.

sources.title: Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) v1.0
sources.relevance: DID method as a scheme, create/resolve/update/deactivate operations, DID controller versus subject, versionId and versionTime resolution, and explicit contrast with non-resolvable UUIDs.

sources.title: ISO 26324:2025 Information and documentation — Digital object identifier system
sources.relevance: DOI syntax, assignment, uniqueness, persistence, granularity, resolution functional component, system metadata, administration by a Registration Authority, and normative relationship to other identifier schemes without replacing them.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 11179-1:2023 Information technology — Metadata registries (MDR) — Part 1: Framework
sources.relevance: Identifier versus linguistically neutral name, scoped identifier within a namespace, registration as identification plus provenance plus quality monitoring, and mapping among registry items.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 6523-1:2023 Information technology — Structure for the identification of organizations and organization parts — Part 1: Identification of organization identification schemes
sources.relevance: Structure for globally unambiguous organisation identification schemes, International Code Designator, and separation of scheme identification from the registration procedure in Part 2.

sources.title: ISO 24619:2011 Language resource management — Persistent identification and sustainable access (PISA)
sources.relevance: PID framework requirements: resolution of one PID to multiple URIs or services, associated metadata, security of PID-to-URI mappings, persistence and granularity of references.

sources.title: HL7 FHIR R5 Datatype Identifier
sources.relevance: Computational identifier tuple of system namespace URI plus value, use codes usual/official/temp/secondary/old, validity period, assigner organisation, and check-digit placement rules.

sources.title: SKOS Simple Knowledge Organization System Reference
sources.relevance: Notations as lexical codes unique within a concept scheme, and mapping properties exactMatch, closeMatch, broadMatch, narrowMatch and relatedMatch for cross-scheme equivalence quality.

sources.title: DOI Handbook
sources.relevance: Operational Handle-based resolution, Global versus Local Handle Service, DOI record types, prefix delegation and RA administration implementing ISO 26324.

sources.title: ARK NAANs and systems
sources.relevance: Name Assigning Authority Number registry, Name Mapping Authority versus assigning authority, collision-free organisational namespaces, and N2T as a multi-scheme resolver.

sources.title: GS1 check digit calculator and identification-key integrity
sources.relevance: Check digit as last digit of fixed-length numeric GS1 keys, exceptions for CPID and GIAI, and GMN check-character pair rather than a single check digit.

sources.title: RFC 9562: Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs)
sources.relevance: 128-bit identifiers requiring no central registration, UUID URN namespace, versions including name-based namespace UUIDs, Nil and Max sentinels, privacy issues of MAC-derived UUIDv1, and explicit non-resolvability relative to DIDs.

bundles.name: Scheme definition
bundles.description: What an identifier scheme is: its identity in master registries, classification as URI scheme, URN namespace, DID method or other managed system, intended purpose and resource class, and the lexical family that distinguishes it from locators and from mere local keys.
bundles.rationale: RFC 3986 treats each scheme as a federated naming system; RFC 8141 and RFC 7595 require a registered name plus a common definition before a string is a valid identifier of that scheme. Without a scheme object, consuming models cannot detect drift.

layers.name: Scheme identity and classification
layers.description: Canonical identifiers for the scheme, human names, registry status and the class of naming system it implements.

findings.name: Canonical scheme identity
findings.description: The scheme must be identifiable independently of any storage format by the identifier assigned in the authoritative registry for its class, with fallback to a governed IRI and then to a Dimension-assigned UUID or ULID. A date is not an identifier.

questions.text: What is the authoritative master-system identifier of this scheme in IANA, ISO, W3C, GS1 or another registration authority, and which registry record is canonical?
What governed global IRI or URN identifies the scheme definition itself when the master registry uses a local token?
If no master-system identifier exists, what UUID or ULID did the adopting Dimension assign, and when was that assignment observed?
What official names, abbreviations and alternate labels must be preserved without treating them as identifiers?

data_elements.name: Scheme identifier
data_elements.description: Authoritative token or IRI for the scheme in its governing registry.

data_elements.name: Governing registry
data_elements.description: Which live registry holds the canonical scheme record.

data_elements.name: Scheme IRI
data_elements.description: Governed IRI for the scheme definition when distinct from the registry token.

data_elements.name: Official name
data_elements.description: Human-readable official name of the scheme, linguistically distinct from the identifier.

data_elements.name: Registry status
data_elements.description: Permanent, provisional, historical, formal, informal or pending-review status as recorded by the governing registry.

artifacts.name: Scheme registry extract
artifacts.description: Snapshot of the IANA, ISO ICD or equivalent registry row that proves the scheme exists and records its status.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Use the registry own scheme or NID token as master identifier; version the extract by retrieval timestamp.

findings.name: Scheme class, purpose and resource scope
findings.description: Schemes differ by whether they are locators, persistent names, decentralised methods or organisation-identification systems, and by the class of resource they are intended to distinguish. RFC 3986 forbids assuming every URI is a locator; RFC 8141 and ISO 26324 require a stated resource class and purpose.

questions.text: Is this scheme a URI scheme, URN namespace, DID method, ISO/IEC 6523 organisation-identification scheme, UUID generator, GS1 key, PID framework, or another classified naming system?
What stated purpose and long-lived utility does the scheme registration claim, and which resource class may receive identifiers?
Does the scheme function as a persistent name, a locator, both, or neither, and is default dereference required to be safe?
In which protocols, industries or communities is the scheme intended to be used, and is use outside that context invalid or merely unsupported?

data_elements.name: Scheme class
data_elements.description: Taxonomy of the naming system.

data_elements.name: Identified resource class
data_elements.description: Kind of referent the scheme is designed to distinguish.

data_elements.name: Name or locator character
data_elements.description: Whether identifiers are names, locators, both or neither.

artifacts.name: Scheme specification
artifacts.description: The RFC, ISO standard, DID method specification or equivalent document that defines purpose and resource class.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Use the specification own identifier (RFC number, ISO reference, DOI of the specification) as master identity.

layers.name: Syntax, integrity and equivalence
layers.description: Lexical production rules, check digits, encoding, canonicalisation and the comparison ladder that decide when two strings are the same identifier.

findings.name: Lexical syntax and checksums
findings.description: A scheme MUST define the syntax of the scheme-specific part so that every valid identifier also matches any encompassing URI grammar. Many numeric schemes add a check digit or check-character pair; some GS1 keys are explicit exceptions.

questions.text: What ABNF, regular expression or other machine-readable production defines a well-formed identifier in this scheme?
Which check-digit or check-character algorithm applies, is the check symbol part of the identifier value, and which keys are exempt?
Which reserved characters act as delimiters inside the scheme-specific part, and when must they be percent-encoded rather than used as data?
Are identifiers required to be opaque, may they be semantic, and is a transcription-safe alphabet recommended?

data_elements.name: Syntax expression
data_elements.description: Machine-readable grammar of valid identifiers.

data_elements.name: Checksum algorithm
data_elements.description: Named check-digit or check-character algorithm, or explicit none.

data_elements.name: Allowed alphabet
data_elements.description: Character repertoire permitted in the assigned name.

artifacts.name: Syntax grammar artefact
artifacts.description: Published ABNF, regex or namespace template that is the syntax of record.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identify by scheme identifier plus grammar version; do not use publication date alone.

findings.name: Canonicalisation, equivalence and presentation forms
findings.description: Two strings may be the same identifier after case folding of scheme or NID, uppercasing of percent-hex, or scheme-specific NSS rules. RFC 8141 forbids decoding percent-encoded octets during URN-equivalence and ignores r/q/f-components. Human display, compact ARK and fully qualified mapping forms must be distinguished from the assigned name. Homoglyphs are not equivalent.

questions.text: What normalisation steps are mandatory before declaring two values URN-equivalent, URI-equivalent or scheme-equivalent, and which components are ignored?
What is the single canonical serialisation producers MUST emit, including lowercase scheme names and uppercase percent-hex?
Which compact, fully qualified, hyphenated, rendered-value or human-display forms are allowed, and which form is used for computational matching?
How does the scheme treat homoglyphs, mixed-script lookalikes and visually identical Unicode that are not octet-equal after normalisation?

data_elements.name: Equivalence profile
data_elements.description: Named comparison ladder or scheme-specific equivalence procedure.

data_elements.name: Canonical form rule
data_elements.description: Required producer serialisation.

data_elements.name: Matching case sensitivity
data_elements.description: Whether the assigned-name is case-sensitive for comparison.

artifacts.name: Equivalence test vectors
artifacts.description: Positive and negative pairs demonstrating scheme, NID, percent-encoding and homoglyph behaviour.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identify each vector by scheme identifier plus stable vector key, not by date.

bundles.name: Authority and governance
bundles.description: Who is mandated to define the scheme, assign names, register sub-namespaces and control changes, including IANA designated experts, ISO registration authorities, DOI Registration Agencies and ARK Name Assigning Authorities.
bundles.rationale: RFC 8141 and RFC 7595 treat assignment as a managed process and require a change controller. ISO/IEC 6523 and ISO 26324 make the registration authority a first-class object. Delegation chains are how collision-free global uniqueness is achieved.

layers.name: Registration authority and mandate
layers.description: The party legally or procedurally mandated to run the scheme or to register schemes of a given class.

findings.name: Registration authority record
findings.description: Each scheme is governed by one or more registration authorities with a documented mandate, start date, and contact. Farance Inc. acts as ISO/IEC 6523 RA; the DOI Foundation is the ISO 26324 RA; IANA designated experts review URN NIDs and URI schemes.

questions.text: Which organisation is the registration authority or designated expert body, and what is its master-system identifier in the party register?
What instrument, standard clause or IANA policy mandates this authority, and from when does the mandate run?
Which evaluation criteria, uniqueness guarantees and publication duties does the authority actually perform?
What happens to the scheme and its assignments if the registration authority is reassigned, loses a domain name used in private schemes, or is dissolved?

data_elements.name: Authority reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the organisation acting as RA or designated expert.

data_elements.name: Mandate
data_elements.description: Instrument and temporal bounds of authority.

data_elements.name: Change controller
data_elements.description: Person or organisation authorised to update the scheme registration.

artifacts.name: Registration-authority appointment
artifacts.description: ICD certificate, IANA expert listing, ISO maintenance-agency notice or equivalent appointment record.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Use the RA organisation identifier plus the scheme or ICD it governs.

findings.name: Scheme registration record and template
findings.description: RFC 7595 and RFC 8141 define templates that must be completed to enter the live IANA registries: purpose, syntax, assignment, security and privacy, interoperability, resolution, contact and references. Informal URN namespaces and provisional URI schemes have lighter but still recorded requirements.

questions.text: What is the current registration status and which procedure (expert review, first-come first-served, IESG approval or fast-track for SDOs) admitted it?
Where is the required security and privacy analysis, including whether the scheme-specific part is privacy-sensitive or correlating?
Which template fields are complete, which are missing, and is a citable specification required for this status?

data_elements.name: Registration status
data_elements.description: Permanent, provisional, historical, formal, informal or pending.

data_elements.name: Registration template payload
data_elements.description: Completed fields of the applicable IANA or ISO template.

data_elements.name: Defining specification citation
data_elements.description: Stable citation of the scheme specification.

artifacts.name: Completed scheme registration template
artifacts.description: The IANA or ISO registration request of record.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identify by scheme name plus registry; version by IANA last-updated timestamp.

layers.name: Namespace delegation and change control
layers.description: Sub-namespace assignment to other authorities, and who may change scheme definitions after registration.

findings.name: Sub-namespace delegation
findings.description: Global uniqueness is often achieved by delegating prefixes: DOI prefixes to Registration Agencies, Handle naming authorities to Local Handle Services, ARK NAANs to organisations, OID arcs to national and private bodies. Assigning authority and mapping or resolution authority may be different parties.

questions.text: What prefix, NAAN, ICD, Handle naming authority or OID arc was delegated, to whom, and under which parent namespace?
Is the Name Assigning Authority distinct from the Name Mapping Authority or resolver operator, and what URL is the official resolver for this delegation?
Under what conditions can a prefix be reassigned or revoked, and how are already-minted identifiers protected?
What evidence shows that assignments under this delegation cannot collide with siblings?

data_elements.name: Delegated namespace token
data_elements.description: Prefix, NAAN, ICD, NID or arc assigned to the delegate.

data_elements.name: Delegate authority
data_elements.description: Organisation receiving the sub-namespace.

data_elements.name: Official resolver for delegation
data_elements.description: Resolver URL registered for the NAAN or prefix.

artifacts.name: Delegated namespace registry entry
artifacts.description: Public NAAN, DOI prefix or ICD register row.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Master identifier is the delegated token in the parent scheme register.

findings.name: Change control and scheme evolution
findings.description: RFC 7595 allows updates by the original registrant or IESG reassignment of provisional schemes; transition to historical requires IESG approval for permanent schemes. Successor schemes such as ISBN-10 to ISBN-13 and UUID RFC 4122 to RFC 9562 must be recorded without silently rewriting old identifiers.

questions.text: Who may update the scheme definition, syntax or resolution behaviour, and which updates require IESG, ISO or RA approval?
Does a successor scheme replace, encapsulate or sit alongside this one, and how are old identifiers rewritten or aliased?
Which previously valid identifiers remain valid after a syntax modernisation, as RFC 8141 promises for RFC 2141 URNs?

data_elements.name: Scheme definition version
data_elements.description: Version of the scheme rules, distinct from identifier values.

data_elements.name: Successor scheme
data_elements.description: Reference to a replacing or superseding scheme.

data_elements.name: Backward compatibility flag
data_elements.description: Whether historic identifiers remain valid.

artifacts.name: Scheme change log
artifacts.description: Approved amendments, status transitions and successor declarations.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each change event has its own identifier; timestamps are RFC 3339 event time plus ingestion time.

bundles.name: Assignment and allocation
bundles.description: The managed process that binds a well-formed identifier to a referent, including uniqueness policy, granularity, assigner identity, evidence and algorithmically generated identifiers that have no central registrar.
bundles.rationale: RFC 8141 states that syntactic correctness is not enough: NID registration plus namespace-specific generation rules are required. ISO 26324 and FHIR Identifier make assigner, uniqueness and granularity explicit. RFC 9562 covers the no-registrar case.

layers.name: Allocation process and uniqueness
layers.description: How names are minted or allocated and the uniqueness contract that allocation must honour.

findings.name: Assignment process
findings.description: Assignment may be organisational, algorithmic (UUID, UUIDv5 name-based), or a mix. RFC 8141 requires a process that is always followed. FHIR records the assigner organisation. Minting cost and rate limits matter for UUIDs and high-volume GS1 keys.

questions.text: Is assignment performed by a registrar, by a local minter under a delegated prefix, by a public algorithm, or by a DID method on a verifiable data registry?
Who assigned the identifier, at what event time, and when was that fact ingested, with evidence?
Under what contract, fee, eligibility or persistence commitment did the registrant obtain the assignment?
If the identifier is derived from a name in another namespace, what canonical octets, hash and Namespace ID were used?

data_elements.name: Assignment method
data_elements.description: Registrar, minter, algorithm or DID method.

data_elements.name: Assigned by
data_elements.description: Organisation or process that performed assignment.

data_elements.name: Assigned at
data_elements.description: Event time of assignment as RFC 3339.

artifacts.name: Identifier assignment record
artifacts.description: Binding of identifier value to referent with assigner, time and evidence.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Prefer the scheme own assignment identifier; else a Dimension UUID. Assignment time is not the identifier.

findings.name: Uniqueness and multiplicity policy
findings.description: RFC 8141 requires that a name is never assigned to more than one resource and never reassigned, even if deprecated. A single resource MAY have several URNs. RFC 3986 notes that the identified resource need not be singular. These policies conflict with telephone-number and some domain reuse practices and must be recorded per scheme rather than assumed.

questions.text: Is uniqueness global, scoped to a namespace, scoped to an assigner, or only statistically probable as with UUIDs?
May one referent hold multiple identifiers in this scheme, and may one identifier ever denote a set or time-varying mapping?
Are identifiers unique only within a local system URI, as in FHIR Identifier.system, or globally unique as assigned-names?

data_elements.name: Uniqueness scope
data_elements.description: Global, namespace, assigner or probabilistic.

data_elements.name: Reassignment allowed
data_elements.description: Whether a retired identifier may later denote a different referent.

data_elements.name: Multiplicity rule
data_elements.description: Allowed identifier-to-referent cardinalities.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Uniqueness policy is a rule set recorded inline on the scheme; it is not a separate file type unless the scheme publishes a dedicated uniqueness policy document, in which case that document is attached via the scheme specification artefact.

layers.name: Referent binding and granularity
layers.description: What is identified, at what grain, and how qualifiers distinguish parts and variants without minting a new assigned name.

findings.name: Referent binding
findings.description: An identifier assignment names a referent. ISO 26324 allows any material or abstract object. DID Core allows any subject the controller decides. The binding must record the referent reference, not embed the referent attributes.

questions.text: What catalogue identifier of the referent is bound, and in which sibling model does that referent live?
If this is a DID or similar, is the controller distinct from the subject, and who may update the binding?
What evidence quality and provenance attach to the claim that this identifier denotes that referent?

data_elements.name: Referent reference
data_elements.description: Pointer to the identified thing in its native model.

data_elements.name: Binding evidence
data_elements.description: Evidence supporting the assignment.

artifacts.name: Assignment evidence pack
artifacts.description: Documents or signed operations proving the binding.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Evidence objects use their own master identifiers; they are referenced from the assignment, not used as the identifier of the referent.

findings.name: Granularity, qualifiers and notations
findings.description: ISO 26324 and ISO 24619 require explicit granularity. ARK qualifiers identify parts and variants. SKOS notations are lexical codes unique within a concept scheme and are not a substitute for URIs. Fragments and f-components identify constituents without changing the assigned name.

questions.text: At what granularity is the identifier defined, and may finer parts be addressed by qualifiers or fragments rather than new assignments?
If a notation or code is used, is it unique only within a concept scheme, and what URI or URN is the preferred computational identifier?
Do content-negotiated, language, format or version variants share the assigned name or require distinct identifiers?

data_elements.name: Granularity level
data_elements.description: Stated grain of the identified object.

data_elements.name: Qualifier syntax
data_elements.description: Rules for parts, variants or fragments.

data_elements.name: Notation
data_elements.description: Lexical code unique within a scheme, if any.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Granularity and qualifier rules are constraints of the scheme definition and assignment record; they are expressed inline unless the scheme publishes a separate qualifier profile.

bundles.name: Identifier lifecycle
bundles.description: Status, validity periods, reservation, temporary use, retirement, reassignment where the scheme permits it, deactivation, split and merge, and time-travel resolution of historical versions.
bundles.rationale: RFC 8141 forbids reassignment; FHIR models temp and old identifiers with periods; DID Core requires deactivate as a method operation and supports versionTime. These rare cases are where catalogue agents fail if the mixin only knows issued versus unused.

layers.name: Status, use and validity period
layers.description: Current state of an identifier and the interval during which it is valid for use.

findings.name: Identifier status model
findings.description: FHIR Identifier.use distinguishes usual, official, temp, secondary and old, and treats temp as a modifier so applications do not mistake a temporary id for a permanent one. URN namespaces still treat retired names as never reusable. DID methods add deactivated. Historical URI schemes are scheme-level, not identifier-level, retirement.

questions.text: What is the current status or use of this identifier, and is that status a modifier that changes matching behaviour?
If the identifier is temporary, what replacement is expected, and may systems persist it beyond the stated period?
Who is authorised to change status, and what evidence is required for retirement or deactivation?

data_elements.name: Identifier status
data_elements.description: Issued, reserved, temporary, official, secondary, old, retired, deactivated or historical.

data_elements.name: Identifier value
data_elements.description: The assigned-name or namespace-specific string unique within the scheme.

data_elements.name: Scheme reference
data_elements.description: The scheme in which the value is assigned.

artifacts.name: Identifier status history
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each transition is a dated event with its own identifier; the identifier value is never used as the event id.

findings.name: Temporal validity and versioning
findings.description: FHIR Identifier.period records when an identifier was valid. DID versionTime and versionId select historical DID documents. Event time of a status change must be stored separately from observation or ingestion time, as RFC 3339 timestamps with seconds and an explicit offset.

questions.text: During which inclusive start and end instants is or was this identifier valid for use, and is a missing end interpreted as ongoing?
Which versionId or versionTime selects the representation that was current at a past instant?
What is the event time of the lifecycle change versus the observation or ingestion time of this record?

data_elements.name: Valid from
data_elements.description: Inclusive start of validity as RFC 3339.

data_elements.name: Valid to
data_elements.description: Inclusive end of validity as RFC 3339, omitted if ongoing.

data_elements.name: Version identifier
data_elements.description: Method-specific version selector for historical resolution.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Validity timestamps and version selectors are inline properties of the identifier assignment and DID URL; they are not independent artefacts unless a DID method materialises versioned documents.

layers.name: Retirement, reuse, split and merge
layers.description: Rare lifecycle cases that differ sharply across schemes and must not be collapsed into a single deleted flag.

findings.name: Retirement, deactivation and reassignment
findings.description: URN uniqueness forbids reassignment even after obsolescence. DID deactivate stops use without necessarily deleting the identifier string. FHIR old marks a former identifier still useful for matching. Telephone-number and some domain practices reuse numbers; those schemes must declare reuse cooling-off explicitly, and this mixin must not silently apply URN rules to them.

questions.text: Does retirement mean the name remains reserved forever, becomes a tombstone that resolves only to metadata, is deactivated, or may be recycled after a cooling-off period?
If reassignment is permitted, what event bound the retired identifier to a new referent, and what collision checks were performed?
Is physical deletion of the assignment record allowed, or must a deactivated or old identifier remain queryable for matching and audit?

data_elements.name: Retirement semantics
data_elements.description: Reserved-forever, tombstone, deactivated, recyclable.

data_elements.name: Reuse cooling-off
data_elements.description: Minimum duration before permitted reuse.

data_elements.name: Tombstone resolution target
data_elements.description: Metadata or notice served after retirement.

artifacts.name: Retirement or deactivation notice
artifacts.description: Public or restricted notice that an identifier is withdrawn, deactivated or recycled.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Notice identity is independent of the identifier value; link both.

findings.name: Split, merge and aliasing
findings.description: Public identities and bibliographic identifiers are sometimes merged or split. SKOS exactMatch is transitive and maps concepts across schemes without asserting owl:sameAs. A resource may carry several URNs for similar or different purposes, which is aliasing rather than merge.

questions.text: If two identifiers were merged, which value survives, which are aliases, and is the merge reversible?
If one identifier was split, which new identifiers were minted for which new referents, and what is the parent identifier?
Are multiple identifiers for one referent true aliases, purpose-specific identifiers, or embeddings of another scheme?

data_elements.name: Surviving identifier
data_elements.description: Canonical identifier after merge.

data_elements.name: Alias set
data_elements.description: Other identifiers treated as aliases.

data_elements.name: Match quality
data_elements.description: exact, close, related or unspecified.

artifacts.name: Merge or split record
artifacts.description: Authoritative event that rewired identifier-to-referent bindings.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Event identifier from the issuing registry; do not reuse either identifier value as the event id.

bundles.name: Resolution and dereference
bundles.description: How a name is turned into locators, metadata, representations or DID documents, including resolver identity, protocols, multi-target PID behaviour, access control and service levels.
bundles.rationale: RFC 3986 separates resolution from dereference. RFC 8141 and ISO 24619 allow resolution to locators, metadata-only, authorised representations or no locator at all. DOI and ARK implement concrete resolver networks.

layers.name: Resolver identity, protocol and coverage
layers.description: Which services claim to resolve which portions of a scheme.

findings.name: Resolution service record
findings.description: A resolver has an endpoint, protocol (HTTP proxy, Handle DO-IRP, DID resolution) and a coverage statement. N2T routes many schemes; DOI Proxy fronts Handle; DID resolvers are method-specific. Scheme operations and default invocation must be documented.

questions.text: What is the resolver endpoint URI, protocol and operator, and is it the official resolver registered for this prefix or NAAN?
Which scheme partitions, prefixes or identifier classes does this resolver cover, and what happens for identifiers outside coverage?
Which operations besides default dereference are defined, including retrieval, metadata, inflections and Handle admin, and which is the default safe operation?
What service level, availability and update-freshness commitments apply to DOI records or equivalent mappings?

data_elements.name: Resolver endpoint
data_elements.description: Network locator of the resolution service.

data_elements.name: Resolution protocol
data_elements.description: Handle, HTTP proxy, DID resolution or other.

data_elements.name: Coverage
data_elements.description: Portion of the identifier space served.

artifacts.name: Resolution service contract
artifacts.description: Terms for dereference at volume, including SLA and acceptable use.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Contract identifier from the operator; link to scheme and coverage.

findings.name: Resolution parameters and DID URL options
findings.description: RFC 8141 r-components are reserved for passing parameters to resolution services and must not affect assigned-name equivalence. DID parameters service, relativeRef, versionId, versionTime and hl distinguish which resource is identified versus how resolution is performed.

questions.text: Does this scheme define r-component or equivalent resolver parameters, or are they still undefined and therefore not to be used?
Which DID URL parameters are supported to select service, relative resource, version or hash integrity?
Which inputs must be part of the identifier URL and which must be resolver options that are not part of identity?

data_elements.name: Resolver parameter profile
data_elements.description: Defined r-component or DID parameter semantics.

data_elements.name: Parameters that affect identity
data_elements.description: Which query parameters are part of the resource identity.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Resolver parameter profiles are reference data on the scheme and resolver; they become artefacts only when published as a separate parameter registry.

layers.name: Dereference results, metadata and access
layers.description: What a successful or authorised resolution returns, and who may obtain representations versus metadata.

findings.name: Multi-target resolution and metadata
findings.description: ISO 24619 requires that a PID framework can resolve one PID to multiple URIs or services and associate metadata. DOI records hold typed values such as URL. RFC 8141 examples include metadata-only resolution for ISNI-like namespaces.

questions.text: To which locators, services or metadata records does this identifier currently resolve, and in what type slots?
If multiple targets exist, how is selection performed by content negotiation, country or service parameter, and is order significant?
What integrity and security controls prevent malicious or accidental modification of PID-to-URI mappings?

data_elements.name: Resolution targets
data_elements.description: Current locator or service values.

data_elements.name: Target type
data_elements.description: Handle type or equivalent slot such as URL or email.

data_elements.name: Mapping last verified
data_elements.description: When the PID-to-URI mapping was last checked.

artifacts.name: PID or Handle record
artifacts.description: Typed resolution record for an identifier.
artifacts.identity_strategy: The identifier value plus scheme is the lookup key; the record still needs its own version identifier for updates.

findings.name: Access-controlled and failing resolution
findings.description: RFC 8141 contemplates authorised retrieval of representations while others receive only metadata, as in a national legal-deposit collection. Resolution may also be undefined for namespaces that identify protocol features rather than retrievable resources. Failure modes and caching must not equate non-retrieval with non-identity.

questions.text: Who may obtain a representation versus metadata versus a mere existence check, and under which exception process?
If the scheme is not intended as a locator, what does software that obtains the identifier do instead of retrieval?
How are not-found, gone, unauthorised and resolver-unavailable distinguished in logs without treating them as identifier invalidity?

data_elements.name: Resolution access policy
data_elements.description: Who may retrieve which result class.

data_elements.name: Non-locator scheme flag
data_elements.description: True when default retrieval is not defined.

artifacts.name: Resolution audit log
artifacts.description: Auditable record of resolution requests where policy requires it, especially bulk or authorised access.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Log event identifiers are ULIDs or equivalent; include event time and ingestion time separately.

bundles.name: Crosswalk, embedding and interoperable forms
bundles.description: Declared equivalences between schemes, embedding of one scheme string inside another, and compact or internationalised forms used on the wire.
bundles.rationale: ISO 26324 states that a DOI does not replace other ISO/TC 46 identifiers but may encapsulate them. SKOS supplies match-quality vocabulary. RFC 7595 shares one scheme registry between URI and IRI. FHIR requires a system URI to compare values.

layers.name: Mapping quality and embedding
layers.description: How identifiers in different schemes are declared equivalent or nested.

findings.name: Cross-scheme mapping
findings.description: Mappings have direction, quality (exact, close, broad, related) and provenance. SKOS exactMatch is transitive and must not be confused with owl:sameAs. Bulk crosswalk tables are often licensed artefacts distinct from pairwise assertions.

questions.text: Which from-scheme identifier is mapped to which to-scheme identifier, in which direction, and with what match quality?
Who asserted the mapping, when, on what evidence, and is it licensed for bulk reuse?
Does this mapping conflict with another mapping, with SKOS integrity conditions, or with a merge record in either scheme?

data_elements.name: From scheme
data_elements.description: Source scheme of the mapping.

data_elements.name: To scheme
data_elements.description: Target scheme of the mapping.

data_elements.name: Match quality
data_elements.description: exactMatch, closeMatch, broadMatch, narrowMatch, relatedMatch or unspecified.

data_elements.name: Mapping licence
data_elements.description: Terms for pairwise or bulk use.

artifacts.name: Bulk crosswalk table
artifacts.description: Pairwise equivalence table between two schemes.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Table identity is dataset identifier plus scheme pair and version; row identity is the from-value in the from-scheme.

findings.name: Embedding and encapsulation
findings.description: RFC 8141 allows NSS to encapsulate hierarchical names from non-URN systems. ISO 26324 describes integrating another scheme character string through DOI syntax or system metadata. FHIR says if the value is a full URI then system SHALL be urn:ietf:rfc:3986. Embedding is not the same as mapping.

questions.text: Does this identifier embed another scheme native string, and what canonicalisation is applied before embedding?
Can the native identifier be recovered losslessly from the encapsulating form, and which form is canonical for matching?
Does the encapsulating scheme claim to replace the native scheme, contrary to ISO 26324 non-replacement rule?

data_elements.name: Embedded scheme
data_elements.description: Native scheme whose string is encapsulated.

data_elements.name: Lossless round-trip
data_elements.description: Whether native form is recoverable.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Embedding rules are constraints on syntax and assignment; they are recorded inline on the scheme unless a dedicated profile is published.

layers.name: Wire forms and interoperability encodings
layers.description: URI versus IRI, compact prefix forms, UUID hex-and-dash versus URN, and FHIR system-plus-value tuples.

findings.name: URI, IRI and compact forms
findings.description: RFC 7595 states IRIs use the same scheme names and the same IANA registry, with RFC 3987 transformations. UUID has hex-and-dash, binary, integer, URN and Microsoft brace forms. Compact ARK omits the resolver host. These forms must not be stored as if they were different identifiers.

questions.text: Is an IRI form defined, which Unicode characters are allowed before percent-encoding, and is UTF-8 mandatory on the wire?
What compact or prefix expansion is recognised, and who governs the prefix registry?
Which alternate serialisations (URN, OID, braces, integer, binary) are accepted as the same UUID or identifier?

data_elements.name: IRI supported
data_elements.description: Whether an IRI form is defined for the scheme.

data_elements.name: Canonical serialisation
data_elements.description: The one form used for storage comparison.

data_elements.name: Prefix expansion rule
data_elements.description: How compact forms expand to full identifiers.

artifacts.name: Form conversion table
artifacts.description: Authoritative examples converting compact, IRI, URN and native forms.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identify by scheme plus vector key.

findings.name: Computational identifier tuple
findings.description: FHIR Identifier shows the operational pattern every consuming model needs: system namespace URI, value unique in that system, optional type, use, period and assigner. Comparison requires knowing the system. Values are case-sensitive unless the system says otherwise.

questions.text: What absolute namespace URI is the system, and what value is unique within it?
Is a coded identifier type recorded for when the system is unknown, without treating type as a substitute for system?
What normalisation is allowed before matching, and is case-insensitive comparison actually safe for this system?

data_elements.name: System namespace URI
data_elements.description: Absolute URI identifying the unique-value set.

data_elements.name: Identifier type
data_elements.description: General category when system is unknown.

data_elements.name: Value case-sensitive
data_elements.description: Whether matching must treat case as significant.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The system-plus-value tuple is inline reference data carried on every identifier instance; it is not a file type.

functions.name: Register identifier scheme
functions.description: Admit a new scheme into the catalogue by recording its master registry identity, specification, syntax, assignment rules, security analysis and change controller.
preconditions: No colliding scheme name in the governing registry.
Template fields required for the requested status are complete.
effects: Creates a scheme object that consuming models may reference.
Starts change-control under the named controller.

functions.name: Validate identifier syntax
functions.description: Check that a candidate string is well-formed for a named scheme, including checksums and encoding constraints, without asserting that it has been assigned.
effects: May emit a canonical form for subsequent matching.

functions.name: Assign identifier
functions.description: Bind a well-formed identifier to a referent under the scheme uniqueness and granularity rules, recording assigner, event time and evidence.
preconditions: Caller is an authorised assigner or minter for the namespace.
Value is well-formed and not assigned to a different referent if uniqueness forbids it.
effects: May mint from a delegated prefix or algorithm.

functions.name: Resolve identifier
functions.description: Given an identifier and resolution options, return locators, metadata, a DID document or an authorised representation according to the scheme.
preconditions: A resolver covering this identifier is known, or the scheme is defined as non-locator.
effects: May be audited when policy requires.

functions.name: Normalise and compare identifiers
functions.description: Apply the scheme equivalence profile to decide whether two strings are the same assigned name.
preconditions: Equivalence profile is recorded on the scheme.

functions.name: Map identifier across schemes
functions.description: Look up or assert a cross-scheme mapping with explicit match quality and provenance.
preconditions: Caller may read or write mappings under the mapping licence.
effects: Must not silently treat exactMatch as owl:sameAs.

functions.name: Retire or deactivate identifier
functions.description: Apply the scheme retirement semantics: forever-reserve, tombstone, DID deactivate, mark old, or schedule reuse.
preconditions: Requested semantics are allowed by the scheme uniqueness policy.
effects: May change resolution targets to metadata-only.

functions.name: Delegate namespace
functions.description: Grant a prefix, NAAN, ICD or arc to another authority and register its official resolver.
preconditions: Caller is the parent registration authority.
effects: Updates public NAAN, prefix or ICD registers.

functions.name: Transfer registration authority
functions.description: Reassign change control or RA mandate when the original registrant is unreachable or an IESG or ISO decision requires it.
preconditions: Authorising body has jurisdiction (IESG, ISO, parent RA).

composition.purpose: Registration authorities, assigners, change controllers and resolver operators are organisations or parties recorded in the party model.
Resolvers are services with endpoints, protocols and SLAs; this mixin adds scheme coverage and PID behaviour only.

composition.target: Catalogue entity models (document, dataset, person, product, location, concept)
composition.purpose: Consuming models carry identifier tuples (scheme plus value plus version of scheme rules) so drift and collision are detectable once.
A scheme formal grammar or SKOS concept scheme may be registered as a model without duplicating ontology stewardship here.
Align URN syntax, uniqueness, namespace registration and resolution; do not claim that every catalogue scheme is a URN.

composition.target: RFC 3986 URI generic syntax and RFC 7595 scheme registration
composition.purpose: Align federated scheme syntax, encoding, operations and IANA status without treating locators as persistent names.
Align assignment, persistence, granularity, resolution and non-replacement of other ISO/TC 46 schemes.
Align method operations, controller/subject split, versioned resolution and deactivation for decentralised schemes.
Align scoped identifiers, namespaces, registration as identification plus provenance plus quality, and mapping among items.
Align ICD-based identification of organisation identification schemes.
Align match-quality vocabulary for cross-scheme identifier and notation mappings.
Align the computational system-plus-value tuple, use codes, period and assigner pattern used in operational systems.
Align no-registrar uniqueness, UUID URN namespace and serialisation variants; record that UUIDs are not resolvable by definition.
Align check-digit practice and documented exceptions for specific key types.
Align multi-target resolution, metadata association and mapping-security requirements for persistent identifiers.

composition.target: Access, ownership and audit service layers
composition.purpose: Scheme definitions are typically public; assignment evidence, bulk crosswalks and authorised representations are owner-gated.

owner_package_requirements: The scheme registrar owns scheme definitions, syntax rules, uniqueness policy and the assignment register of record.
Registrants own facts about their own referents and may not alter scheme rules.
Resolver operators own endpoint and SLA records but not the meaning of assigned names.
Mapping stewards own crosswalk assertions they publish and the licences that govern bulk export.
dimension.namespace_guidance: Place this mixin at NAV.XCT.IDS. Identify schemes by master-registry token or IRI under a catalogue namespace derived from the Dimension; never use a date as an identifier. Assigned identifier values remain in their native scheme namespace and are referenced, not rewritten, except where a documented encapsulating form is the canonical computational representation.

canonicalization_rules: Scheme names and URN NIDs are compared case-insensitively and stored lowercase.
Percent-encoded hex digits in canonical forms use uppercase; percent-encoded octets are not decoded when testing URN-equivalence.
UUID text forms used for matching are lowercase hex-and-dash or the scheme stated canonical serialisation.
r-components, q-components, f-components and equivalent resolver parameters are not part of the assigned name.
Event time and ingestion time are both stored; neither is used as an identifier.
patch_rules: Patches to scheme syntax or uniqueness policy require the change controller and must record backward-compatibility.
Assignment records are append-only for status history; corrections are new events, not silent rewrites.
Provisional scheme updates follow the original registrant or IESG reassignment rules; permanent-to-historical transitions follow the governing registry.
Crosswalk patches must preserve match-quality and provenance; they must not upgrade closeMatch to exactMatch without new evidence.
compatibility_rules: Identifiers valid under a prior syntax edition remain valid if the scheme specification promises grandfathering, as RFC 8141 does for RFC 2141 URNs.
Successor schemes (for example UUID RFC 9562 versus RFC 4122) coexist until a documented cut-over; old values are not rewritten.
Encapsulating schemes MUST NOT be treated as replacements of native ISO/TC 46 or other native schemes.
DID Core v1.0 remains the alignment target until a later Recommendation is adopted; v1.1 drafts are recorded as emerging, not as conformance claims.

identity_priority: Authoritative master-system identifier from IANA, ISO, W3C, GS1 or the scheme RA.
Governed global identifier or IRI of the specification or registry row.
UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension when no master identifier exists.
artifact_rules.timestamp_rule: All event times and observation or ingestion times SHALL be recorded as RFC 3339 timestamps with seconds and an explicit offset or Z; a date is not an identifier.
artifact_rules.serial_naming_rule: Serial artefacts (registry extracts, assignment records, crosswalk tables, status histories) use the scheme or identifier master id plus a monotonic serial or version id, never a date-only name.
artifact_rules.integrity_rule: PID-to-URI mappings, assignment evidence and bulk crosswalks MUST carry integrity protection appropriate to the scheme (Handle administration controls, signatures, checksums or hashlinks) so accidental or malicious modification is detectable.

policies: Scheme definitions and public registry status are readable by default; assignment evidence, authorised representations and licensed bulk crosswalks are restricted to the respective owner.
Uniqueness and reassignment policy of the scheme of record prevails over catalogue convenience; URN-like schemes never recycle names.

Physical deletion of assignment records is forbidden where retirement semantics require tombstones, old identifiers for matching, or audit; otherwise deletion follows the records-retention sibling after cooling-off.
Agents MUST NOT construct URNs from native non-URN names unless they implement the namespace-specific canonicalisation rules.

read: Any catalogue agent may read public scheme definitions, syntax, uniqueness policy and official resolver endpoints.
Assignment values and referent bindings are readable according to the referent owner access policy.
Bulk crosswalks require the mapping licence scope.
create: Scheme registrar or delegated RA creates scheme and namespace records.
Authorised minters and DID controllers create assignments.
Mapping stewards create crosswalk assertions they are licensed to publish.
update: Change controller updates scheme rules with a compatibility record.
Assigners and DID controllers update status, resolution targets and DID documents per method operations.
IESG or parent RA may reassign provisional change control.
delete: Assigned names are not deleted under URN uniqueness; they are retired or deactivated.
Physical delete of scheme records that still have live assignments is forbidden.
Historical URI scheme status is a status change, not a row delete, in the IANA-aligned register.

roles.name: Scheme registrar
responsibilities: Own scheme definitions and the assignment register of record.
Ensure syntax, uniqueness and persistence policies are explicit.
Publish AGENTS.md bootstrap fields for this mixin.

roles.name: Registration authority
responsibilities: Evaluate applications, assign ICDs, prefixes or NAANs, and maintain the public scheme or namespace register.
Appoint or recognise delegates and official resolvers.

roles.name: Registrant / assigner
responsibilities: Request and maintain assignments for their referents.
Supply evidence and keep resolution targets current.

roles.name: Resolver operator
responsibilities: Operate endpoints, honour coverage and SLA, and protect PID-to-URI mappings.
Distinguish identity parameters from resolver options.

roles.name: Mapping steward
responsibilities: Assert cross-scheme mappings with quality and provenance.
License bulk crosswalks and record conflicts.

roles.name: Designated expert
responsibilities: Review permanent URI scheme and URN NID registrations against RFC 7595 and RFC 8141.
Note colliding uses rather than silently overwriting them.

access.default_rule: Scheme metadata is public; assignment evidence, authorised representations, resolution audit logs and bulk crosswalks default to owner-only until a licence or exception is granted.
exceptions: National-library or similarly authorised resolution may return metadata to the public and representations only to entitled callers.
Third-party registration of an observed-in-the-wild unregistered URI scheme may identify both the registering party and the scheme creator.
Emergency IESG or parent-RA reassignment of a contact-lost provisional scheme.
audit_requirements: Log scheme registration, namespace delegation, assignment, status change, resolver-endpoint change and bulk crosswalk export with event time, actor and ingestion time.
Resolution requests are audited when the scheme or contract requires it, especially for access-controlled representations.

coverage.claim: This mixin covers the defensible operating surface of identifier schemes as governed naming systems: identity in live registries, syntax and checksums, authority and delegation, assignment, rare lifecycle cases, resolution and crosswalk. It is not a universal catalogue of every industry identifier and does not claim conformance of any particular deployment to the aligned standards.

checklist.notes: Master-registry tokens, governed IRIs and Dimension UUID/ULID fallback are modelled; dates are excluded as identifiers.
Reservation, issuance, temp/old/official use, retirement, deactivation, reassignment, split/merge, successor schemes and historical URI scheme status are in scope.
Governed-by, delegates, assigns, resolved-by, maps, embeds and alias/merge relations are explicit.
Assignment time, validity period, versionTime/versionId, event versus ingestion time, and cooling-off durations are modelled as RFC 3339 instants or durations.
Assigner, mapping asserted-by, evidence packs and registration templates carry provenance.
Registrar versus registrant versus resolver operator versus mapping steward is separated; DID controller versus subject is recorded.
Syntax, checksums, equivalence profiles and SKOS integrity conflicts are first-class.
Public scheme metadata versus restricted assignment evidence, authorised resolution and licensed bulk crosswalks, plus audit.
URN forever-reserve versus recyclable schemes versus DID deactivate versus physical-delete prohibition for live assignments.
URI/IRI, UUID serialisations, compact ARK, FHIR system-plus-value, DOI encapsulation and SKOS match quality.
RFC 8141 never-reassign is the URN default; conflicting reuse policies must be declared per scheme.
RFC 3986 distinction plus PID multi-target and metadata-only cases.
ICD, NAAN, DOI/Handle prefix and change-control succession.
RFC 7595 privacy-sensitive scheme parts, UUIDv1 MAC leakage, DID privacy goals; national ID schemes remain out of content scope.

known_omissions: ITU-T E.164 telephone numbering, number portability and reuse cooling-off were not fetched as primary text and are flagged as a likely reuse-policy omission.
ITU-T X.660 / ISO/IEC 9834 OID arc administration is only indirectly supported via urn:oid and FHIR oid, not as a full RA model.
W3C CURIE and prefix.cc community prefix governance lack a primary fetch in this run.
NISO, DataCite kernel, ORCID and ISNI merge procedures are discovered via IANA NID entries but not specified here as first-party operating manuals.
DID v1.1 Candidate Recommendation Snapshot of 5 March 2026 is emerging and not the alignment target.
Handle DO-IRP 2022 is cited from the DOI Handbook rather than fetched as a DONA primary.
Jurisdiction-specific civil identifiers (national ID, tax ID) are out of content scope; scheme-level privacy rules still apply if such a scheme is registered.
Quantum-resistant identifier cryptography and ledger-specific DID method suites are not specified.
conflicts: RFC 8141 uniqueness never reassigns a name; FHIR old/temp and many telecom/domain schemes permit reuse or former-identifier matching. Record the scheme policy; do not globalise URN rules.
RFC 8141 restricts URNs to ASCII with percent-encoding; RFC 3987 IRIs share the URI scheme registry. A scheme may have both forms only if its specification says so.
ISO 26324: a DOI does not replace other ISO/TC 46 identifiers even when it encapsulates their strings.
DID Core: UUIDs are not resolvable or cryptographically verifiable; treating urn:uuid as a DID method is a conflict.
SKOS exactMatch versus owl:sameAs: mappings of identifiers or notations are not identity of referents.
RFC 8141 r-components are syntactically defined but SHOULD NOT be used until their semantics are standardised.
Microsoft COM GUID little-endian layout versus RFC 9562 network byte order.
Historical URI schemes remain in IANA with status historical; absence from common use is not deletion.
regional_assumptions: IANA and ISO registries are treated as globally authoritative for the scheme classes they govern; national bibliographic or eID schemes may add regional RAs not listed here.
ARK NAAN registry hosting at CDL with mirrors at NLM and BnF is the current operational assumption, not a metaphysical lock-in.
GS1 check-digit rules as published by GS1 AISBL are used; national GS1 member organisations may add allocation policy.
English official names are stored as names; other language designations belong in a naming-convention sibling aligned with ISO/IEC 11179-5.
adversarial_checks: Would a date such as 2026-08-22 be accepted as a scheme or assignment identifier? No; identity priority forbids it.
Would constructing a URN ISBN from a native ISBN without namespace canonicalisation be allowed? No; RFC 8141 forbids unaware construction.
Would marking a DID deactivated be treated as deleting the identifier string and allowing reuse? No; deactivation is not URN-style deletion nor automatic recycling.
Would two strings that differ only in a q-component be treated as different URNs? No; RFC 8141 ignores r/q/f-components for equivalence.
Would a bulk SKOS exactMatch export be treated as merging organisations or works in the referent models? No; mapping quality is not referent identity.
